item.title: Inclusive commercial real estate redevelopment in racialized urban markets: Evidence from West Baltimore
item.description:
Qingfang Wang, Yang Li, Lyneir Richardson, Emma Gonzalez MacRoberts
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261503517
Drawing on two shopping-center redevelopment projects in West Baltimore, this study examines how inclusive commercial real estate (CRE) redevelopment can be assembled in racialized urban markets through institutional reconfiguration. Using in-depth interviews, document analysis, investor surveys, and field observation, the analysis identifies a linked set of mechanisms through which inclusive CRE operates in practice: expanded participation through small-dollar equity investment, blended capital arrangements that redistribute risk across actors and time horizons, governance enacted through leasing and relationship work, and valuation practices that integrate financial viability with community outcomes. Social enterprise coordinates these mechanisms by linking community participation, CRE development capacity, and public and mission-aligned capital. The study advances urban scholarship by specifying how inclusive redevelopment is produced through concrete institutional mechanisms embedded within capital-intensive property markets, offering a framework for analyzing equity-oriented commercial redevelopment beyond binary distinctions between market-led and community-based development.

item.title: The conspicuous rise of tarifa zero as an urban policy: Unpacking the opportunities and contradictions of fare-free public transport in Brazil
item.description:
Daniel Santini, Wojciech Kębłowski
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261504606
Brazil currently hosts the world’s largest concentration of fare-free public transport (FFPT) systems, with 145 municipalities having adopted tarifa zero . This article examines the rise of FFPT not as a narrow pricing reform but as a multidimensional urban policy. Drawing on a systematic mapping of the nationwide landscape of FFPT, document analysis and a multiple-case study, we trace the chronology and geography of FFPT diffusion, unpack its financial architecture and interrogate the political rationales shaping its design. Our findings show that FFPT has expanded through distinct phases, from early experiments in the 1990s to a post-pandemic surge, with adoption patterns shaped by metropolitan clustering and inter-municipal policy mobility. While small and mid-sized cities dominate numerically, larger urban centres increasingly determine demographic impact and political salience, bringing attention to substantial technical, fiscal, institutional, political and infrastructural challenges to implementing the policy at scale, which shape both feasibility and distributive outcomes. Operationally, FFPT succeeds when paired with governance reforms – particularly the shift from passenger-based to supply-based remuneration. Politically, FFPT’s uptake cuts across ideological lines, driven less by doctrinal commitments than by systemic transport crises and electoral incentives, a pattern that calls for a multidisciplinary analytical framework that reaches beyond questions of transport pricing. Yet design choices – partial versus universal coverage, equity-oriented versus operator-oriented models – determine whether FFPT advances social justice or entrenches private capture.
